title: Azure Virtual Desktop vs. Windows 365: PaaS Flexibility vs. SaaS Simplicity
summary: This lesson draws the line every Microsoft-stack EUC engineer needs to draw cleanly: Azure Virtual Desktop (AVD) is a PaaS you architect and operate, while Windows 365 Cloud PC is a SaaS you provision and hand to a user. You'll compare their ownership models, session types, licensing shapes, and pricing predictability, then survey Windows 365's delivery modes — Boot, Switch, and Frontline — at a high level so you can recognize them in a customer conversation before Module 5 goes deep on administering them.
objectives: Explain the fundamental service-model difference between AVD (PaaS) and Windows 365 (SaaS)
Contrast pooled multi-session AVD desktops with Windows 365's personal-only Cloud PC model
Describe how licensing and pricing predictability differ between the two platforms
Identify at least three scenarios where AVD is the better fit and three where Windows 365 wins
Summarize what Windows 365 Boot, Switch, and Frontline each do at a high level
Recognize Windows 11 Enterprise multi-session as the OS unique to AVD pooled desktops

quiz.q: Which statement best captures the core architectural difference between Azure Virtual Desktop and Windows 365?
options: AVD only supports Windows 10; Windows 365 only supports Windows 11

AVD is a PaaS where the customer owns and manages the session hosts inside their own Azure subscription; Windows 365 is a SaaS where Microsoft manages the Cloud PC's underlying infrastructure end to end
AVD is on-premises only; Windows 365 is cloud only
There is no meaningful difference — they are the same service with different marketing names
quiz.why: AVD gives you a control plane managed by Microsoft but session hosts that live as VMs in your own subscription — you patch, size, and image them. Windows 365 abstracts all of that away: you buy a per-user Cloud PC SKU and Microsoft runs the infrastructure behind it, exposed to you mainly through Intune.

quiz.q: A customer needs pooled, multi-session desktops shared across shift workers to minimize per-user compute cost. Which platform natively supports this session model?
options: Windows 365 Cloud PC, because it is always the cheaper option
Neither platform supports multiple users sharing one desktop
Azure Virtual Desktop, because it supports pooled host pools running Windows 11 Enterprise multi-session
Windows 365 Frontline, because it is licensed per virtual machine
quiz.why: AVD is the only one of the two with a true pooled, multi-session desktop model — multiple users share session hosts running Windows 11 Enterprise multi-session, an OS SKU that does not exist outside AVD. Windows 365 Cloud PCs (outside Frontline's shared mode) are always personal, one-to-one desktops.

quiz.q: Why is Windows 365 often described as offering more predictable cost than AVD?
options: Windows 365 has no licensing requirements at all
AVD cannot be metered or billed
Windows 365 desktops never need to be resized, so cost never changes
Windows 365 uses a fixed, per-user, per-month price that bundles compute, storage, and the Cloud PC license into one SKU
quiz.why: Windows 365's defining pitch is a flat per-user, per-month price for a given Cloud PC size — you know your bill before the month starts. AVD's cost is consumption-based across compute, storage, and networking, which is more flexible and can be cheaper at scale but requires active cost management (covered in Module 3).

quiz.q: Which Windows 365 capability lets a user boot a physical device (or thin client) directly into their Cloud PC instead of a local Windows desktop?
options: Windows 365 Boot
Windows 365 Switch
Windows 365 Frontline
Windows 365 Link
quiz.why: Windows 365 Boot signs a device directly into a user's Cloud PC at startup, bypassing the local Windows desktop entirely — well suited to shared or kiosk-style hardware. Switch lets a user toggle between their local desktop and Cloud PC using Task View; Frontline is a licensing/session model for shift-based shared access.

quiz.q: A regulated customer wants engineers to keep full administrative control over the OS image, patch cadence, and networking of their virtual desktops, and is comfortable managing that complexity in exchange for flexibility. Which platform better fits this requirement, and why?
options: Windows 365, because SaaS is always more secure
AVD, because as a PaaS it exposes the session host VM, image pipeline, and networking configuration directly to the customer's own Azure subscription and admins
Neither platform allows any customer control
Windows 365 Frontline specifically, because it is the only mode with admin control
quiz.why: AVD's PaaS model is exactly the fit when a customer wants deep control: they own the golden image, the Azure Compute Gallery, the VNet, and the patch cadence. Windows 365 deliberately trades that control away for simplicity, which is the wrong trade for a customer that needs fine-grained infrastructure ownership.

quiz.q: In three to five sentences, describe a realistic scenario where a single organization would deploy BOTH Azure Virtual Desktop and Windows 365 side by side rather than choosing only one.
quiz.answer: A mid-size company might run AVD pooled host pools with Windows 11 Enterprise multi-session for its call-center and shift-based staff, where dense, cost-optimized multi-user desktops make sense and IT already has Azure and networking expertise. The same company could issue Windows 365 Cloud PCs to executives, remote contractors, or M&A-acquired staff who need a fast, predictably priced, personal desktop with minimal IT setup and Intune-only management. Some may also use Windows 365 Frontline for warehouse kiosks that need Boot-style dedicated sign-in. This mixed model lets IT match each user population to the platform that fits its session type, budget model, and management overhead instead of forcing everyone onto one platform.
quiz.why: AVD and Windows 365 are not mutually exclusive — most real Microsoft-stack EUC estates run both, matching pooled/PaaS AVD to cost-sensitive multi-session populations and SaaS Windows 365 to users who need simplicity, personal desktops, or predictable per-user billing. This mirrors the decision framework built out fully in Lesson 5.

body_markdown:
## Two Microsoft Platforms, One Very Different Bet

Microsoft sells two very different answers to "give my users a Windows desktop in the cloud": **Azure Virtual Desktop (AVD)** and **Windows 365**. They are built on overlapping technology — both ultimately deliver a Windows session over RDP-family protocols, both integrate with Microsoft Entra ID and Intune, both can run Windows 11 — but they make opposite bets on who owns the complexity. AVD bets that you *want* control and are willing to operate infrastructure for it. Windows 365 bets that you want a desktop the way you buy a Microsoft 365 mailbox: as a fixed-price SaaS SKU you provision and stop thinking about.

Getting this distinction right is the single most common conversation a VDI/EUC engineer has with a customer or stakeholder, so this lesson builds the comparison cleanly before Module 3 goes deep on AVD infrastructure and Module 5 goes deep on Windows 365 administration.

## Azure Virtual Desktop: PaaS You Architect

AVD is a **platform-as-a-service**. Microsoft manages the control plane — the broker that matches users to sessions, the web/gateway endpoints, the diagnostics pipeline — but you, the customer, own everything downstream of that: the **session host virtual machines**, which live as ordinary Azure VMs inside your own subscription and resource group.

That ownership means you are responsible for, and get to customize:

- **The OS image** — including **Windows 11 Enterprise multi-session**, an OS SKU that exists *only* for AVD and allows many users to share one VM's compute simultaneously (a genuine architectural difference from Windows 365, which never multiplexes users onto one instance outside Frontline's shared mode).
- **Networking** — your VNet, your egress path, your Private Link and RDP Shortpath configuration (Module 3).
- **Sizing and scaling** — VM SKU choice, autoscale plans, GPU options (Lesson 4 of this module).
- **Patching and image lifecycle** — Azure Compute Gallery versioning, your own cadence.

Session types in AVD split into **pooled** (many users share a set of interchangeable multi-session hosts; non-persistent by default, cheapest per-user cost) and **personal/dedicated** (one VM assigned permanently to one user; behaves like a traditional persistent desktop). Both run inside host pools that you deploy, size, and monitor.

## Windows 365: SaaS You Provision

Windows 365 Cloud PC removes almost all of that. You buy a **Cloud PC license** (a fixed SKU defined by vCPU/RAM/storage, e.g., 4 vCPU / 16 GB / 128 GB) for a named user, and Microsoft provisions and runs the underlying VM for you — you never see or manage an Azure subscription hosting it (in the standard **Microsoft-hosted network** option; the **Azure Network Connection**, or ANC, option lets you inject the Cloud PC into your own VNet for the networking control that some customers still need, without handing you the VM itself).

Critically, Windows 365 Cloud PCs are **always personal** — one Cloud PC, one user, persistent, full state retained between sessions. There is no pooled, multi-session Windows 365 desktop for a general population; the closest thing is **Frontline**, which lets a *license pool* be shared by shift-based users who are never signed in simultaneously, not concurrent-use multiplexing on one VM.

Management for Windows 365 flows almost entirely through **Microsoft Intune** — provisioning policies, resize actions, restore points — which Module 5 covers in administrator depth.

## Windows 365's Delivery Modes at a Glance

Three named capabilities show up repeatedly in Windows 365 conversations. At this stage you only need to recognize them; Module 5 covers administering them:

| Capability | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Windows 365 Boot** | Signs a physical device (including shared/kiosk hardware) directly into a user's Cloud PC at device startup, bypassing the local Windows desktop |
| **Windows 365 Switch** | Lets a user toggle fluidly between their local Windows desktop and their Cloud PC using Windows 11 Task View, as if it were another virtual desktop |
| **Windows 365 Frontline** | A licensing and session model for shift-based or task workers, offering *dedicated* mode (a Cloud PC held for a worker during their shift) and *shared* mode (a pool of Cloud PCs drawn from a smaller license pool than the user count) |

## Licensing and Cost Shape

The cost *model*, not just the cost amount, is the real decision driver:

- **Windows 365**: a flat **per-user, per-month price** per Cloud PC size. You know your bill in advance; there is no consumption variability to manage. This is attractive to finance teams and to IT organizations without deep cloud cost-management maturity.
- **AVD**: **consumption-based** across compute (VMs, which you can stop/deallocate or autoscale), storage (OS disks, FSLogix profile storage), and networking egress. This can be materially cheaper at scale — especially with pooled multi-session density and autoscale — but requires active cost engineering, which Module 3 Lesson 5 covers.

Both platforms layer on top of **existing Windows/Microsoft 365 entitlements** — Windows 365 requires its own per-user Cloud PC license; AVD requires a qualifying Windows/Microsoft 365 license (typically E3/E5 or equivalent) plus the Azure infrastructure spend itself, a distinction fully unpacked in Module 1 Lesson 5's licensing lesson.

## When Each One Wins

**AVD tends to win when:** the population needs pooled multi-session economics (call centers, education labs, task workers at scale); the organization has existing Azure/networking expertise and wants infrastructure control; workloads need GPU, custom images, or complex network topology; or cost optimization at scale matters more than administrative simplicity.

**Windows 365 tends to win when:** users need a **personal**, persistent desktop with minimal setup; IT wants Intune-only management with no Azure subscription to operate; billing predictability is a hard requirement; or the rollout needs to happen fast — contractors, M&A onboarding, BYOD replacement — without a networking or imaging project attached.

Most real Microsoft-stack estates run **both**, matched to population — exactly the mixed-platform thinking Lesson 5's decision framework will formalize, and that Module 5 Lesson 5 revisits with full Windows 365 administrative depth.

## What's Next

You now have the Microsoft-native half of the 2026 VDI landscape. The next three lessons widen the lens to the platforms your customers may already have standing estates on — Citrix DaaS and Omnissa Horizon — plus the GPU and niche-vendor space, before Lesson 5 gives you the scoring framework to choose between all of them.

slides.narration: Welcome to Module 2, where we survey the 2026 VDI platform landscape. We start inside Microsoft's own portfolio, because most learners will meet these two platforms first. Azure Virtual Desktop and Windows 365 both deliver a Windows desktop from the cloud, but they make opposite bets on who owns the infrastructure complexity. By the end of this lesson you'll be able to explain that difference clearly to a customer or a hiring manager.

slides.title: Two Very Different Service Models
bullets: AVD: platform-as-a-service, you own the session host VMs
Windows 365: software-as-a-service, Microsoft owns the infrastructure
Both integrate with Microsoft Entra ID and Intune
The split determines who does the engineering work
slides.narration: Azure Virtual Desktop is a platform as a service. Microsoft runs the broker and gateway, but the session host virtual machines live in your own Azure subscription, and you own them. Windows 365 is a software as a service. You buy a Cloud PC license per user and Microsoft runs the infrastructure behind it end to end. Both plug into the same identity and management fabric, Entra ID and Intune, but the ownership split is the whole story.

slides.title: Session Types: Pooled vs. Personal
bullets: AVD pooled: many users share multi-session hosts
Windows 11 Enterprise multi-session exists only in AVD
AVD personal: one VM per user, persistent
Windows 365: always personal, one Cloud PC per user
slides.narration: AVD supports pooled host pools where many users share multi-session hosts running Windows 11 Enterprise multi-session, an operating system edition that exists nowhere outside AVD. AVD also supports personal host pools, one VM permanently assigned to one user. Windows 365 only ever offers a personal model: one Cloud PC per user, persistent, with full state retained. There is no general pooled multi-session Windows 365 desktop.

slides.title: Windows 365's Delivery Modes
bullets: Boot — signs a device straight into a Cloud PC at startup
Switch — toggle between local desktop and Cloud PC via Task View
Frontline — dedicated or shared modes for shift-based workers
Full administration covered in Module 5
slides.narration: Three Windows 365 capabilities come up constantly. Boot signs a physical device straight into a user's Cloud PC at startup, useful for shared or kiosk hardware. Switch lets a user move fluidly between their local desktop and their Cloud PC using Windows 11's Task View. Frontline is a licensing and session model for shift workers, with a dedicated mode and a shared mode drawing from a smaller license pool. At this stage, just recognize these names; Module 5 covers administering them.

slides.title: Cost Model: Predictable vs. Consumption-Based
bullets: Windows 365: flat per-user, per-month price
AVD: consumption-based across compute, storage, egress
AVD can be cheaper at scale with pooled density and autoscale
AVD requires active cost engineering; Windows 365 does not
slides.narration: Windows 365 charges a flat per-user, per-month price for a given Cloud PC size, so your bill is known before the month starts. AVD bills consumption based, across compute, storage, and network egress. That gives AVD more room to be cheaper at scale, especially with pooled multi-session density and autoscale, but it demands active cost engineering, which we cover in Module 3.

slides.title: Where AVD Wins
bullets: Pooled multi-session economics at scale
Existing Azure and networking expertise in-house
GPU, custom imaging, or complex network needs
Cost optimization matters more than simplicity
slides.narration: AVD tends to win when the population fits pooled multi-session economics, like call centers or education labs, when the organization already has Azure and networking skills, when workloads need GPU or custom imaging or complex networking, and when cost optimization at scale outweighs the convenience of a fully managed service.

slides.title: Where Windows 365 Wins
bullets: Personal, persistent desktop needed fast
Intune-only management, no Azure subscription to run
Billing predictability is a hard requirement
Contractors, M&A onboarding, BYOD replacement
slides.narration: Windows 365 tends to win when users need a personal, persistent desktop and need it fast, when IT wants Intune-only management without operating an Azure subscription, when predictable billing matters to finance, and for fast-turnaround scenarios like contractor onboarding, M&A integration, or replacing a BYOD device with a managed Cloud PC.

slides.title: Most Estates Run Both
bullets: Match platform to population, not to a single company standard
Pooled task workers on AVD, executives on Windows 365
Frontline for shift-based kiosk scenarios
Lesson 5 formalizes this into a scoring framework
slides.narration: In practice, most real Microsoft-stack organizations run both platforms side by side, matching each user population to the platform that fits its session type and budget model rather than forcing everyone onto one standard. Lesson 5 of this module turns that instinct into a repeatable scoring framework you'll reuse in the Module 7 capstone.
